title: Branches and prediction
objectives: Explain branch prediction and remove a branch from a hot loop.

screens.title: Guess before you know
screens.prose: A CPU guesses each branch before it knows the answer. Model the guess as a counter c from 0 to 3. It guesses taken (T) at 2 or 3. It moves up on T and down on N, stopping at 0 and 3.

state.caption: T is taken, N is not taken.

screens.question: The counter starts at 1. Tap every step where it guesses wrong.

hints.text: At c = 1 the guess is N.
After the first T the counter is 2, so it guesses T.
Wrong at steps 0, 3 and 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the counter step by step.

byKey.c1: After step 0 the counter is 2, so step 1 guesses T: right.
byKey.c5: Before step 5 the counter is 1, so it guesses N: right.
byKey.c0: At c = 1 the counter guesses N, but the branch is taken.
byKey.c4: After one N the counter is only down to 2, so it still guesses T.

explain.text: Before each step the counter reads 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1: wrong at steps 0, 3 and 4. A wrong guess throws away about 15 to 20 cycles of work; we use 5 ns. Three **mispredictions** cost 15 ns.

screens.title: A loop branch
screens.prose: A loop of four passes ends with an N, twice over. Step through it and watch the counter. Wrong steps turn bold.

state.caption: The counter starts at 1. Move the slider to run the first branch.

frames.caption: The counter starts at 1. Move the slider to run the first branch.
Step 0: counter 1 guesses N, branch is T: wrong. Wrong so far: 1.
Step 1: counter 2 guesses T, branch is T: right. Wrong so far: 1.
Step 2: counter 3 guesses T, branch is T: right. Wrong so far: 1.
Step 3: counter 3 guesses T, branch is N: wrong. Wrong so far: 2.
Step 4: counter 2 guesses T, branch is T: right. Wrong so far: 2.
Step 5: counter 3 guesses T, branch is T: right. Wrong so far: 2.
Step 6: counter 3 guesses T, branch is T: right. Wrong so far: 2.
Step 7: counter 3 guesses T, branch is N: wrong. Wrong so far: 3.

screens.question: How many wrong guesses over the 8 steps?

hints.text: The first T is wrong because the counter starts at 1.
Each N that ends a loop is wrong.
Steps 0, 3 and 7.

feedback.correct: Three: the start and the two loop exits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step through to the end and read the caption.

byKey.two: Count step 0 too: the counter starts at 1 and guesses N.
byKey.four: After the N at step 3 the counter is 2, so step 4 guesses T: right.

explain.text: Once warm, the counter misses only the N that ends each loop. One N moves it from 3 to 2, so it still guesses T next. That is why a **two-bit** counter suits loop branches.

canvas.caption: Step 7: counter 3 guesses T, branch is N: wrong. Wrong so far: 3.

screens.title: Random data
screens.prose: A loop runs `if (x >= 128)` over bytes. On random bytes the branch is taken about half the time, in no order.

params.title: Seeded run, 10,000 outcomes, about half taken
lines: two-bit counter, outcomes in random order:  5,064 wrong (50.6%)
the same outcomes sorted, all N then all T:      2 wrong

screens.question: Over 1,000,000 random bytes, at 5 ns a wrong guess, how many ms does the branch add?

hints.text: What fraction of guesses is wrong on random data?
The seeded run shows about half.
$10^6 \times 0.5 \times 5$ ns.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply elements, the wrong fraction and the cost.

byKey.all: 5 ms would mean every guess is wrong. Random data gets about half right.
byKey.micro: 2,500 is in microseconds. Divide by 1,000 for ms.

explain.text: About half the guesses are wrong: $10^6 \times 0.5 \times 5$ ns is 2.5 ms. Sorted, the same bytes give 2 wrong guesses in 10,000. The order of the data, not the code, sets the cost.

screens.title: A mask instead of a branch
screens.prose: We can remove the branch. A comparison gives 1 or 0, and the minus turns that into a mask.
screens.question: For x = 200, what is `-(x >= 128)`?

options.text: −1: every bit set, so the mask keeps x
1: so the mask keeps only the lowest bit
options.why: `x >= 128` is 1, and the minus makes it −1, all bits set.
200 is at least 128, so the comparison is true.

hints.text: What is `x >= 128` for x = 200?
It is 1, and `-1` in two's complement has every bit set.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the comparison, then negate it.

explain.text: `-(x >= 128)` is −1 (all ones) or 0, so `x & mask` is x or 0. The sum is the same, with no jump to predict. The price is a negation and an AND on every element.

screens.title: When the mask loses
screens.prose: Here is a desk run of both loops. The figures are quoted from one machine, not measured in this app.

params.title: A desk run: one 2.3 GHz server core, ns per element

state.caption: 32,768 random bytes summed 20,000 times, g++ 13.3 and clang++ 18.1. One machine, rounded to two figures.

screens.question: When is the branchless mask loop slower than the branch?

options.why: The mask does extra work on every element, so it loses when the branch is well predicted.
Random data is where the branch is wrong half the time: 6.3 ns against 2.2 to 2.5.
On random data the mask wins: 2.2 to 2.5 ns against 6.3.

hints.text: Compare the mask with the branch line by line.
Sorted, the branch is 1.5 to 1.8 ns.
1.5 to 1.8 beats 2.2 to 2.5.

feedback.correct: On sorted data: the branch is nearly free there.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the sorted branch with the mask.

byKey.b: The blurt is that branchless always wins. A well predicted branch costs less than the mask's extra work.

explain.text: Sorted, the branch costs 1.5 to 1.8 ns and the mask 2.2 to 2.5 ns, so the mask loses. On random data it wins by about 4 ns. Remove a branch only when it is hard to predict.

screens.title: The compiler got there first
screens.prose: At `-O1` the branch loop runs at the same speed sorted or not. This app compiles at `-O1` too.

params.title: A desk run: one 2.3 GHz server core, ns per element

state.caption: 32,768 random bytes summed 20,000 times, g++ 13.3 and clang++ 18.1. One machine, rounded to two figures.

screens.question: Why does the order of the data stop mattering?

options.text: The compiler turned the branch into a conditional move

options.why: No flag changes your data. The compiler changes the code.

options.text: The predictor learns random data at `-O1`
options.why: The predictor is hardware, and flags cannot change it.

options.text: The loop is removed as dead code
options.why: The sum is used, so the loop stays.

hints.text: What would make sorted and random data cost the same?
No jump means nothing to predict.
A conditional move picks a value without jumping.

feedback.correct: A conditional move: there is no branch left to mispredict.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is left to predict.

explain.text: At `-O1` both compilers emit a conditional move, so there is no branch to guess. That is why this lesson quotes a desk run. You cannot see the effect in this app's `-O1` build.

screens.title: Count the wrong guesses
screens.prose: Write the two-bit counter. The starter is a one-bit predictor: it guesses the last outcome.
screens.question: Fix `mispredicts` to model the two-bit counter that starts at 1.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Ten hidden tests, including an empty history, a single T, a loop branch and the alternating history.

hints.text: Keep a counter from 0 to 3 instead of one bit.
The guess is taken when `counter >= 2`.
Count a miss when the guess differs. Then move the counter up on T and down on N, stopping at 0 and 3.

feedback.correct: That's it. Guess, compare, then move the counter.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

explain.text: The one-bit starter flips its guess after every surprise, so a loop exit costs it two misses. The two-bit counter needs two surprises in a row to flip.

screens.title: The cost of guessing
screens.prose:
Every cost today was one product:

$$\text{extra time} = n \times p_{\text{wrong}} \times 5\text{ ns}$$

Regular is not the same as predictable. `TNTN...` fools a two-bit counter every time. Real predictors keep a history and learn it.
screens.question: 1,000,000 branches, wrong 10% of the time: how much extra time?

options.why: You charged every branch, not the 10% that are wrong.
That is the random case, wrong 50% of the time.
Check the zeros: $10^5$ misses at 5 ns is 0.5 ms.

hints.text: How many guesses are wrong?
100,000 wrong guesses.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the three factors.

explain.text: $10^6 \times 0.1 \times 5$ ns is 0.5 ms. The wrong fraction is the number to measure.

screens.title: Drill: predictors
screens.prose: Drill: about 90 seconds each. Say the counter values aloud first. The 5 ns cost is a round figure: know it to a power of ten. The two-bit counter starts at 1. A one-bit predictor guesses the last outcome and starts at N.
screens.question: Fill in the wrong guesses.

hints.text: Write the counter under each letter.
After warming up, TTN costs the two-bit counter one miss per N.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: The first T and the two N: 3.
byKey.r1c1: The first T, then one miss per N: 1 + 10.
byKey.r2c1: N is right, the first T is wrong at c = 0, and the second T is wrong at c = 1.
byKey.r3c1: The counter swings between 1 and 2 and is wrong every time.
byKey.r4c1: One bit misses every change of outcome: 6.
byKey.r5c1: The first T and each of the three N.

explain.text: A two-bit counter pays once to warm up, then once per surprise. Alternation beats it every time. A one-bit predictor pays twice for every loop exit.

screens.title: Follow-up: a switch on the message type
screens.prose: The interviewer asks whether to make the handler's switch branchless. Types arrive in random order: 70% adds, 15% cancels, 15% trades.
screens.question: The best guess is always 'add'. At 5 ns a miss, what does the switch cost per message, in ns?

widget.accept: 1.5: wrong 30% of the time, at 5 ns.

hints.text: How often is 'add' the wrong guess?
Cancels and trades: 30%.

feedback.correct: 1.5 ns a message: 0.3 ms a second at 200,000 messages.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the wrong fraction by 5 ns.

byKey.all: Only the 30% that are not adds are wrong.
byKey.half: 0.75 ns counts only one of the two other types.
byKey.seventy: 3.5 ns charges the adds, which the guess gets right.

explain.text: The guess is wrong 30% of the time: $0.3 \times 5 = 1.5$ ns a message. At 200,000 messages a second that is 0.3 ms a second, 0.03% of a core. Measure before you optimise: this branch is not the problem.

ideas: The CPU guesses each branch; a wrong guess throws away 15 to 20 cycles, about 5 ns.
A two-bit counter predicts loops well and random data badly: about half wrong.
A branchless mask wins only on hard-to-predict data, and the compiler may already have done it.
summary.trap: Believing branchless always wins: on sorted data the branch is nearly free.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the counter: 1, 0, 0, 0.

byKey.two: At c = 1 the guess is N, so the first N is right.
byKey.zero: The counter is at 0 when the T comes, so it guesses N.

explain.text: The counter goes 1, 0, 0, 0, guessing N each time. Only the final T is wrong.

quiz.prose: A branch on random data is wrong half the time. Each wrong guess costs 5 ns.
quiz.question: How many ms does it add over 10,000,000 elements?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the three factors and convert ns to ms.

explain.text: $10^7 \times 0.5 \times 5$ ns is $2.5 \times 10^7$ ns, which is 25 ms.

quiz.prose: The loop `if (x >= 128) sum += x;` runs at `-O0`.
quiz.question: Which data makes it cheapest?

options.why: Random order is where the guess is wrong half the time.
Alternation is regular, but a two-bit counter is wrong every time.

feedback.correct: Sorted: the counter is almost never wrong.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which order lets the counter settle?

explain.text: Sorted data is all N then all T, so the counter is wrong about twice. Alternation is the worst case for it.

quiz.prose: A hot loop checks a flag that is true 99.9% of the time.
quiz.question: Should you rewrite it branchless?

options.text: No: it is almost always predicted, so the branch is nearly free

options.why: A predicted branch costs about nothing. Only wrong guesses cost.
The mask adds work on every pass.

feedback.correct: No. Measure first, and keep a well predicted branch.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How often is the guess wrong?

explain.text: Wrong 0.1% of the time, the branch costs $0.001 \times 5 = 0.005$ ns a pass. A mask would cost more than that.
